title: What is the difference between a deep copy and a shallow copy?
description: Reference semantics: spread, Object.assign, structuredClone, recursion pitfalls, and why copying matters for React state immutability.

data.text: **Question:** What is the difference between a deep copy and a shallow copy?

A **shallow copy** duplicates only the top level: the new object/array is independent, but its nested values are still **shared references** to the originals — mutating `copy.a.b` changes `original.a.b`. A **deep copy** duplicates the whole tree, so nothing is shared. In JavaScript, `{ ...obj }`, `Object.assign({}, obj)`, `arr.slice()`, and `Array.from(arr)` are shallow. `structuredClone(obj)` is the built-in deep copy (recursively clones plain data, Dates, Maps, Sets, ArrayBuffers — fails on functions, DOM nodes, class prototypes, and cyclic-aware in ways that matter). JSON round-tripping (`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))`) is a common hack that silently drops undefined, functions, Dates (→ strings), and blows up on circular references.

**Why copies exist at all:** JavaScript assigns objects **by reference** — `const b = a` makes both names point to one object. Many patterns (React state, undo history, immutable stores) require 'a new object that differs by one field' without touching the old one.

**Shallow copy tools:**
- `{ ...obj }` / `Object.assign({}, obj)` — copies own enumerable props one level; nested objects, arrays inside are shared
- `arr.slice()` / `[...arr]` / `Array.from(arr)` — new array, same element references
- `Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(obj))` — same one-level semantics
- Nested state update in React still needs manual spreads per level (`{ ...state, user: { ...state.user, name } }`) — that's shallow copying applied deliberately at every level you intend to change

**Deep copy tools:**
- `structuredClone(x)` — native, handles cycles, many built-ins; cannot clone functions/class instances (throws DataCloneError), DOM nodes, getters/setters (values are read, not copied)
- Hand-written recursive clone for controlled shapes; libraries (`cloneDeep`) for complex graphs with special cases
- JSON round-trip: fast to write, lossy — Date → string, undefined/function dropped, NaN → null, throws on cycles

**When to deep vs shallow:**
- Immutable state update → shallow copy each level along the changed path (cheap, preserves shared untouched subtrees — this is structural sharing, what Immutable.js/Immer optimize)
- Full isolation (snapshot, worker postMessage, offline queue) → deep clone
- Never deep-clone casually in hot paths — cost is O(tree size); clone once at the boundary

**Subtleties:**
- Spread ignores non-enumerable props and prototype chain — the copy is a plain object (loses class methods)
- Maps/Sets: spread gives a new container with same references; structuredClone deep-copies contents
- Symbols: spread copies symbol-keyed own enumerable props; JSON ignores them
- Cyclic structures: spread is fine (shallow); structuredClone handles cycles; JSON.stringify throws

data.title: Where shallow copies bite, and choosing the right tool
Don't deep-clone to 'fix' mutability bugs
data.text: structuredClone everywhere hides the real issue — you pay O(tree) per update and still share nothing, destroying structural sharing benefits. For immutable state, do deliberate per-level shallow copies (or use Immer), and reserve deep cloning for true isolation boundaries: workers, snapshots, persisted queues.

Interviewers want to assess:
- Precise definitions and the reference-sharing consequence of shallow copies
- Knowing the toolset: spread (shallow), structuredClone (deep, with limits), JSON (lossy hack)
- The React connection: per-level spread, immutability bugs from shared nesting
- Cost awareness: deep copying is O(tree); prefer structural sharing

items: Spreading one level and mutating nested arrays/objects — still aliases the original
Using JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) and losing Dates, undefined, functions, or crashing on cycles
Deep-cloning entire large state on every keystroke
Replacing a nested object wholesale instead of spreading it (dropping sibling fields)
Expecting spread to preserve class prototypes or copy getters
Mutating a shared subtree that another copy also references — the state desync bug

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Shallow copy: new top level, shared nested references
Spread/Object.assign/slice are shallow; structuredClone is the deep-copy standard
JSON round-trip is lossy — Dates, undefined, functions, cycles
Immutable updates: shallow-copy each changed level; deep-clone only at isolation boundaries
data.takeaway: Copies in JavaScript are about reference graphs: know exactly which edges are new and which still point to the original.
